T1: Consumers will adopt a consumer CPR home training product because they view it as a private, convenient way to learn a life-saving skill, and they trust the brand and regulatory endorsement. Who benefits: Individuals and families who need to be prepared for cardiac emergencies; Laerdal benefits from premium pricing and brand extension.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from viewing CPR as a professional/medical task to a personal, routine health skill when it is delivered in a private, home environment and accompanied by clear, regulated guidance.. How value is captured: Laerdal sells a branded, regulated home kit at a premium price, and can license the brand to other consumer health devices.. Assumptions: Consumers trust the brand and regulatory endorsement more than generic home CPR resources.; Home CPR training is perceived as a private, discreet activity suitable for households.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a branded, regulated product.. Predictions: In a test offering a branded home CPR kit, purchase intent among households will be higher than for an identical unbranded kit.; Consumers will report higher confidence in performing CPR correctly when the kit bears a recognized brand and carries regulatory certification..

T2: Consumers will adopt a consumer CPR home training product because they need to be prepared for cardiac emergencies, and they trust the brand and regulatory endorsement as a signal of safety. Who benefits: Individuals and families who need to be prepared for cardiac emergencies; Laerdal benefits from brand extension and premium pricing.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from viewing CPR as a professional/medical task to a personal, routine health skill when they perceive the product as regulated, trusted, and backed by a reputable brand.. How value is captured: Laerdal sells a branded, regulated home kit at a premium price, and can license the brand to other consumer health devices.. Assumptions: Consumers associate brand and regulatory endorsement with safety and efficacy.; Home CPR training is perceived as a necessary, life-saving skill rather than a luxury.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that is trusted by health authorities.. Predictions: In a test offering a branded home CPR kit, purchase intent among households will be higher than for an identical unbranded kit.; Consumers will report higher confidence in performing CPR correctly when the kit bears a recognized brand and carries regulatory certification..

Test "Branded vs Unbranded Home CPR Kit Purchase Test" between T1; T2. Method: Randomized controlled online survey with a choice between a branded home CPR kit (Laerdal brand, regulatory certification) and an identical unbranded home CPR kit. Participants are recruited from households in the United States with at least one adult member. Each participant sees one of the two kits and is asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and to state the maximum price they would pay.. Sample: Proposed sample: 500 households (1,000 participants) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect the U.S. population.. Measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score for the branded kit versus the unbranded kit. Secondary measure: maximum price participants would pay for the branded kit.. Predictions: T1: Branded kit will achieve a higher average purchase intent score than the unbranded kit, and the difference will be statistically significant (p < 0.05).; T2: Unbranded kit will achieve a higher average purchase intent score than the branded kit, and the difference will be statistically significant (p < 0.05).. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for the branded kit is at least 1.5 points higher than the unbranded kit and the difference is statistically significant, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CPR training). If the difference is less than 1.5 points or not statistically significant, do not invest in a consumer proposition at this time.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence shows Laerdal already offers a branded home CPR program (CPR Anytime) and that consumers are prepared to perform CPR in homes, but it does not demonstrate that consumers will purchase a branded home kit at a premium price. A controlled test is needed to measure purchase intent and price sensitivity. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence shows Laerdal already offers a branded home CPR program (CPR Anytime) and that consumers are prepared to perform CPR in homes, but it does not demonstrate that consumers will purchase a branded home kit at a premium price. A controlled test is needed to measure purchase intent and price sensitivity. Target customer: Individuals and families who need to be prepared for cardiac emergencies, particularly those who currently lack access to professional training.. Value proposition: A branded, regulated home CPR kit that delivers private, convenient training and can be shared with family members, leveraging Laerdal’s reputation and regulatory endorsement to justify a premium price.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Branded vs Unbranded Home CPR Kit Purchase Test (500 households, 10 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and price sensitivity before committing to a consumer product.. Uncertainty: Whether consumers will actually purchase the branded kit at a premium price, and whether the perceived value of brand and regulation outweighs price sensitivity.. Would change if: If the test shows the branded kit achieving a purchase intent difference of at least 1.5 points and a statistically significant p-value, we would proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition.; If the test shows the unbranded kit achieving higher purchase intent or that price sensitivity is high, we would reconsider the investment.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Branded vs Unbranded Glove Choice Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice experiment with simulated purchase.. Sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region. Participants receive a description of a glove that is functional but branded with Ansell's logo and a lifestyle/medical claim (e.g., 'style that protects' or 'medically certified for diabetes'). They are asked to indicate which they would purchase and at what price they would pay.. Measure: Purchase intent: binary choice (Would you buy this glove?) and maximum price willingness to pay. Secondary: self‑reported likelihood to buy multiple pairs for different activities.. Predictions: T1: Participants exposed to the lifestyle/branded claim will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than those exposed to the unbranded functional claim.; T2: Participants exposed to the medical/branded claim will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than those exposed to the unbranded functional claim.. Decision rule: If the lifestyle/branded group exceeds the medical/branded group by ≥15 percentage points in purchase intent, we conclude T1 is more likely. If the medical/branded group exceeds the lifestyle/branded group by ≥15 percentage points, we conclude T2 is more likely. If the difference is ≤15 percentage points, the theories are equally plausible and further testing is needed.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Branded vs Unbranded Glove Choice Test (or a similar choice experiment) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a lifestyle‑branded claim versus a functional‑unbranded claim.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for differentiated gloves and the willingness to pay a premium for lifestyle branding remain uncertain. Evidence of actual purchase behavior is needed to confirm demand.. Would change if: If the test shows the lifestyle/branded group significantly outperforms the functional/branded group by ≥15 percentage points, we would shift focus to a medical‑branded proposition (supporting T2).; If the test shows no significant difference or the functional/branded group outperforms, we would reconsider the investment or explore other alternatives.. Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Styled vs Reusable Glove Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from outdoor recreation and homeowner demographics. Each participant sees one of two product descriptions for a protective glove: (A) Styled, fashion-forward design marketed as a versatile outdoor accessory; (B) Reusable, convenient glove marketed as a single, durable item for everyday tasks. After viewing the description, participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 400 participants (200 outdoor recreation enthusiasts, 200 homeowners) recruited via panel providers, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each product variant.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for the styled variant compared to the reusable variant.; T2: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for the reusable variant compared to the styled variant.. Decision rule: If the styled variant achieves a purchase intent score at least 5 points higher than the reusable variant (i.e., styled ≥ reusable +5) and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting outdoor recreation. If the reusable variant achieves the higher score, pursue a reusable kit proposition. If neither variant meets the threshold, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Franke Coffee Systems should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its professional coffee machines, and identify what public evidence would justify that investment.. Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Energy-Efficient Testo Instruments" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions. Sample: 500 U.S. homeowners and small business owners (200 per arm) recruited via panel, balanced for income and heating usage. Measure: Average WTP in euros for a Testo energy-efficient instrument (e.g., thermal camera) compared to a comparable non-energy-efficient instrument. Predictions: T1: Higher WTP for the energy-efficient instrument in regions with higher average heating costs; T2: Higher WTP for the energy-efficient instrument in regions with higher professional trade concentration and lower trust in consumer brands. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the energy-efficient Testo instrument is at least 20% higher than the WTP for a comparable non-energy-efficient instrument in the target region, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, consider other alternatives. If the difference is less than 5 percentage points, the evidence is insufficient to justify investment.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners and small businesses seeking to reduce heating costs and improve home comfort, supported by evidence of rising energy prices and consumer willingness to pay a premium for energy-efficient instruments. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners and small businesses seeking to reduce heating costs and improve home comfort, supported by evidence of rising energy prices and consumer willingness to pay a premium for energy-efficient instruments. Target customer: Homeowners and small business owners in regions with high heating costs and growing awareness of energy efficiency. Value proposition: Energy-efficient Testo instruments that directly lower heating costs and improve home comfort, positioned as a professional-grade solution for DIY and small business users. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (500 U.S. homeowners, 8 weeks, €15,000) to test the premium demand hypothesis; use results to decide whether to develop a consumer line or pursue other alternatives. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and the actual willingness to pay for energy-efficient instruments are uncertain; the decline in the Consumer segment and reduced promotional funding may limit immediate demand. Would change if: If the survey shows willingness to pay for an energy-efficient Testo instrument is below 10% of the price of a comparable non-energy-efficient instrument, the investment case weakens. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Measure: Purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price willingness to pay for a Testo kit.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the energy efficiency condition compared to the status condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the status condition compared to the energy efficiency condition.. T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home gas detector if it is marketed as a safety necessity and backed by clear regulatory compliance, because they currently lack awareness and trust in CO alarms. Who benefits: Homeowners and renters who face CO risks from cooking, heating, or ventilation.. Why behaviour changes: Increased awareness of CO poisoning risks and a trusted recommendation from a medical/safety brand will motivate purchase beyond price sensitivity.. How value is captured: Dräger can charge a premium for a compliant, certified device and capture recurring revenue through accessories and service, leveraging its safety brand credibility.. Assumptions: Regulatory environment allows consumer CO detector certification.; Consumers trust safety brand recommendations over price alone.; Marketing can effectively communicate safety benefits to a non-technical audience.. Predictions: In a test offering a compliant CO detector at a price comparable to non-compliant models, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than for a non-compliant alternative.; Surveyed buyers will cite safety concern as the primary reason for purchase..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home gas detector if it is positioned as a lifestyle accessory or fashion item, because they view safety devices as status symbols rather than purely functional items. Who benefits: Style-conscious consumers who value design and brand identity.. Why behaviour changes: Exposure to design-focused marketing and social proof (e.g., influencer endorsements) shifts perception from utilitarian to aspirational, increasing willingness to pay a premium.. How value is captured: Dräger can command higher prices for design-led products and capture recurring revenue through accessories, limited editions, and brand extensions, leveraging its safety reputation as a design asset.. Assumptions: Consumers associate safety brands with premium aesthetics.; Social media and influencer marketing can effectively influence purchase decisions for non-functional products.; Regulatory compliance can be satisfied without compromising design.. Predictions: In a test offering a design-focused CO detector at a premium price, purchase intent will be at least 20% higher than for a functional, low‑priced alternative.; Buyers will cite design and brand appeal as the primary reason for purchase..

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Safety vs Lifestyle Positioning" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase. Participants view two product concepts for a home gas detector: (A) Safety‑focused version marketed as a medical‑grade, regulatory‑compliant device for CO and gas detection; (B) Lifestyle‑focused version marketed as a design‑led, premium‑priced accessory with aesthetic features. Each concept includes a price point and a brief description. Participants indicate whether they would purchase each concept and state the primary reason for their choice.. Sample: 500 adults in Germany (n = 250 per condition) recruited via an online panel to ensure demographic diversity.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and primary reason for choice (open‑ended). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Safety‑focused concept will achieve at least 15% higher purchase intent than lifestyle‑focused concept, and safety concern will be the primary reason for purchase.; T2: Lifestyle‑focused concept will achieve at least 20% higher purchase intent than safety‑focused concept, and design/brand appeal will be the primary reason for purchase.. Decision rule: If the purchase intent difference between the two concepts is at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop the higher‑intent proposition. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, consider both concepts but prioritize safety‑focused positioning due to evidence of consumer demand for safety‑branded devices.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CO detector) that emphasizes safety compliance, regulatory certification, and trust in a medical/safety brand. Begin with a small-scale pilot test to validate purchase intent and primary purchase reason before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand for home gas detectors, safety positioning, or lifestyle appeal. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CO detector) that emphasizes safety compliance, regulatory certification, and trust in a medical/safety brand. Begin with a small-scale pilot test to validate purchase intent and primary purchase reason before scaling. Target customer: Homeowners and renters in Germany who face CO risks from cooking, heating, or ventilation.. Value proposition: A compliant, certified home gas detector that provides reliable safety monitoring, backed by Dräger’s safety brand credibility, offering peace of mind and potential recurring revenue through accessories and service.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed 8‑week, €18,000 online choice‑based conjoint survey with 500 German adults to measure purchase intent and primary reason for each concept.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for home gas detectors and the willingness to pay a premium for safety‑branded products are uncertain. Regulatory feasibility for consumer CO detectors is also unknown.. Would change if: If the pilot shows purchase intent below 10% or if the primary reason for purchase is not safety concern, we would reconsider the safety‑focused approach and explore lifestyle positioning.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for design‑led safety products, we would revise the strategy to prioritize lifestyle positioning.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt home water testing kits because they want to monitor their drinking water quality independently and gain peace of mind, leading to repeat purchases of test strips and accessories. Who benefits: Individual homeowners and renters who are concerned about water quality but currently rely on utility or professional testing.. Why behaviour changes: Growing public awareness of water quality issues (e.g., lead, pesticides, bacteria) and a desire for control over personal health creates a willingness to invest in DIY testing.. How value is captured: Hach can capture value through recurring sales of test strips, accessories, and potentially bundled subscription services for data analysis or follow-up testing.. Assumptions: Consumers trust DIY testing results enough to act on them; Price sensitivity is manageable for a premium product; Distribution channels (hardware stores, online) are accessible to target consumers. Predictions: Willingness to pay for a premium test kit will exceed the cost of a single test; Repeat purchase rate for test strips will be higher than for one-time use; Consumer surveys will show intent to purchase a home water testing kit within the next 12 months.

T2: Consumers will adopt home water testing kits because they need to comply with local water quality regulations or safety standards, making DIY testing a legal requirement rather than a voluntary choice. Who benefits: Homeowners and renters in regions with strict water quality laws who must test their water to ensure compliance.. Why behaviour changes: Regulatory pressure and the need to avoid fines or legal action create a mandatory need for accurate water testing, shifting behavior from voluntary to required.. How value is captured: Hach can capture value through compliance-focused sales of test kits, accessories, and potentially subscription services for regulatory reporting.. Assumptions: Regulatory bodies enforce water quality testing in target regions; Consumers are aware of and comply with these regulations; Hach's products meet the required standards for regulatory compliance. Predictions: Sales of compliance-focused test kits will increase in regions with strict water quality laws; Consumers will purchase kits at higher volumes when marketed as required by regulation; Regulatory bodies will report increased adoption of DIY testing kits in compliance regions.

Test "DIY vs Professional Installation Choice Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase and willingness-to-pay questions. Participants are randomly assigned to either a DIY scenario (low-cost, easy installation) or a Professional scenario (guaranteed installation, premium price). Both scenarios present Kingspan's insulation product at a fixed price point (e.g., £150 for a 2m x 1m board). Participants indicate their preferred choice and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 500 UK homeowners (250 per arm) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and energy concern levels.. Measure: Primary measure: proportion of participants choosing the DIY scenario vs Professional scenario. Secondary measure: average maximum price participants would pay for each scenario.. Predictions: T1: At least 55% will choose the DIY scenario and be willing to pay up to £150.; T2: At least 55% will choose the Professional scenario and be willing to pay up to £150.. Decision rule: If DIY share ≥ 55% AND Professional share ≤ 45%, conclude T1 is supported. If Professional share ≥ 55% AND DIY share ≤ 45%, conclude T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, conclude no clear preference.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for DIY home insulation, leveraging Kingspan’s existing direct-to-consumer channel and DIY resources. Target customer: UK homeowners seeking to improve home energy efficiency and reduce heating bills, particularly those who view DIY as a viable option.. Test "Consumer Intent Test: Willingness to Pay for Home Water Test Kit" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question. Participants are recruited from a panel matching the demographic distribution of homeowners in regions with varying water quality regulations. Participants are shown a product description of a home water test kit and asked: "How much would you pay for a single test kit?" They also indicate whether they would purchase it if it were required by a local regulation (T2) or if they already own a test kit (T1).. Sample: 500 participants (150 from regions with strict water quality laws and 150 from regions with moderate laws), balanced for age, gender, and income.. Measure: Average WTP for a single test kit (EUR) and binary purchase intent (required by regulation vs. already own kit).. Predictions: T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in regions with strict water quality laws compared to moderate laws.; T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in regions with strict water quality laws compared to moderate laws.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for a single test kit in the strict-law group exceeds the average WTP in the moderate-law group by at least €10, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting that segment. T1: Consumers will adopt home water testing kits because they want to monitor their drinking water quality independently and gain peace of mind, leading to repeat purchases of test strips and accessories. Who benefits: Individual homeowners and renters who are concerned about water quality but currently rely on utility or professional testing.. Why behaviour changes: Growing public awareness of water quality issues (e.g., lead, pesticides, bacteria) and a desire for control over personal health creates a willingness to invest in DIY testing.. How value is captured: Hach can capture value through recurring sales of test strips, accessories, and potentially bundled subscription services for data analysis or follow-up testing.. Assumptions: Consumers trust DIY testing results enough to act on them; Price sensitivity is manageable for a premium product; Distribution channels (hardware stores, online) are accessible to target consumers. Predictions: Willingness to pay for a premium test kit will exceed the cost of a single test; Repeat purchase rate for test strips will be higher than for one-time use; Consumer surveys will show intent to purchase a home water testing kit within the next 12 months.

T2: Consumers will adopt home water testing kits because they need to comply with local water quality regulations or safety standards, making DIY testing a legal requirement rather than a voluntary choice. Who benefits: Homeowners and renters in regions with strict water quality laws who must test their water to ensure compliance.. Why behaviour changes: Regulatory pressure and the need to avoid fines or legal action create a mandatory need for accurate water testing, shifting behavior from voluntary to required.. How value is captured: Hach can capture value through compliance-focused sales of test kits, accessories, and potentially subscription services for regulatory reporting.. Assumptions: Regulatory bodies enforce water quality testing in target regions; Consumers are aware of and comply with these regulations; Hach's products meet the required standards for regulatory compliance. Predictions: Sales of compliance-focused test kits will increase in regions with strict water quality laws; Consumers will purchase kits at higher volumes when marketed as required by regulation; Regulatory bodies will report increased adoption of DIY testing kits in compliance regions.

Test "Consumer Intent Test: Willingness to Pay vs Regulatory Compliance" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Measure: 1) WTP for a premium home water test kit (e.g., $25 for 50 test strips). 2) Intent to purchase a kit marketed as required by regulation versus a voluntary health-monitoring kit.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the voluntary kit in the region with strict laws exceeds the WTP for the compliance kit by at least $5, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for voluntary health monitoring. If the average WTP for the compliance kit in the region without strict laws exceeds the WTP for the voluntary kit by at least $5, prioritize a compliance-focused proposition. If both regions show similar WTP for the voluntary kit, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Product Messaging Test: Premium vs Convenience Framing" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with targeted recruitment of home office professionals and small retailers. Participants view one of two product descriptions for a Franke consumer machine (A300 or Mythos). Description A emphasizes professional-grade coffee quality, brand prestige, and suitability for modern workspaces. Description B emphasizes convenience, low maintenance, and space efficiency. Participants then indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale (1‑2 ).. Sample: 400 respondents (200 per condition) recruited via professional networking sites and retail forums to ensure target demographics.. Measure: Average WTP (eur) and purchase intent (7-point scale) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Premium condition will achieve higher average WTP and purchase intent than convenience condition, indicating demand for quality-driven pricing.; T2: Convenience condition will achieve higher average WTP and purchase intent than premium condition, indicating demand for low-maintenance, space‑friendly solutions.. Decision rule: If premium condition average WTP ≥ €80 and exceeds convenience condition by at least 15 points, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition. If convenience condition average WTP ≥ €80 and exceeds premium condition by at least 15 points, focus on a convenience‑driven proposition. If neither condition meets its threshold, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and a choice-based conjoint to measure premium willingness to pay and cost-saving willingness to pay.. Sample: 500 U.S. homeowners who have a central air conditioning system and have a programmable thermostat, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: 1) Premium willingness to pay: maximum price a respondent would pay for a Belimo smart thermostat compared to a competitor's smart thermostat. 2) Cost‑saving willingness to pay: maximum annual energy‑cost savings a respondent would accept as a trade‑off for a Belimo smart thermostat versus a competitor's smart thermostat.. Predictions: T1: Respondents will indicate a premium willingness to pay at least 20% above the competitor's price and a cost‑saving acceptance of at least $200 annual savings.; T2: Respondents will indicate a premium willingness to pay at least 15% above the competitor's price and a cost‑saving acceptance of at least $200 annual savings.. Decision rule: If the premium willingness to pay for Belimo exceeds the competitor's price by at least 20% AND the cost‑saving acceptance of $200 annual savings is met, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If either condition is not met, do not invest in a consumer expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Test "Home Gas Detector Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online controlled experiment with two between‑subjects conditions. Participants view a product description of a compliant home CO detector (T1) or a design‑focused home gas detector (T2). Both versions are priced at a premium comparable to non‑compliant alternatives. Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not likely to 7‑very likely) and state the primary reason for purchase.. Sample: 400 adults (200 per condition) recruited via an online panel to match demographic distribution of target consumers (homeowners, renters, age 25‑55).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑90) and primary reason for purchase (open‑ended).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and primary reason of safety concern for the compliant version than for the design version.; T2: Higher purchase intent and primary reason of design/brand appeal for the design version than for the compliant version.. Decision rule: If the design version’s purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher than the compliant version and at least 20 percentage points above the baseline (1), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the compliant version’s purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher and the design version is not significantly better, focus on safety‑driven B2B expansion. If neither condition meets the thresholds, do not invest.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Differentiated Consumer Ice Machine" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from residential households in Japan. They view a mock Hoshizaki countertop ice machine with three variants: a standard compact model, a premium-priced energy-efficient model, and a basic model. Each variant is described with features such as energy rating, brand reputation, and price. Participants indicate their maximum price they would pay for each variant and whether they would purchase it.. Sample: Proposed sample: 400 Japanese residential households (200 per variant) recruited via an online panel. Recruitment target: households with at least one adult member aged 18-65 who makes purchasing decisions for home appliances.. Measure: Primary measure: average maximum price participants indicate they would pay for each variant. Secondary measure: binary purchase intent (would buy) for each variant.. Predictions: T1: Average maximum price for the standard compact variant will be the highest, and purchase intent will be low across all variants.; T2: Average maximum price for the premium-priced variant will be the highest, and purchase intent will be low across all variants.. Decision rule: If the average maximum price for the premium-priced variant exceeds the average maximum price for the standard compact variant by at least 15% (e.g., premium price ≥ 1.15 × standard price), conclude T2 is supported and recommend a premium-priced consumer proposition. If the premium price does not exceed the standard price by 15% or if purchase intent for the premium variant is low, conclude T1 is supported and recommend a convenience-focused consumer proposition. If neither condition is met, suggest further market research.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Once treated water leaves the plant, it can come in contact with various components within the distribution system that potentially alter the quality of the water before it reaches consumers. This makes it hard to guarantee quality for the customer and emphasizes the importance of testing samples in the field.

Drinking water test kits (home test kits) are widely available at hardware stores and the internet, allowing customers to independently assess their drinking water quality at their tap. These kits provide several tests, including: pesticides, bacteria, lead, copper, nitrate, nitrite, iron, chlorine, pH, hardness, and alkalinity.

Home test kit results should be considered an initial step, not a final result. A poor water quality result by a kit should be confirmed with follow-up analyses by a laboratory that uses state-of-the-art instruments, certified methods, and quality control measures to ensure accuracy and reliability.

T1: Consumers will adopt home water testing kits because they want to monitor their drinking water quality independently and gain peace of mind, leading to repeat purchases of test strips and accessories. Who benefits: Individual homeowners and renters who are concerned about water quality but currently rely on utility or professional testing.. Why behaviour changes: Growing public awareness of water quality issues (e.g., lead, pesticides, bacteria) and a desire for control over personal health creates a willingness to invest in DIY testing.. How value is captured: Hach can capture value through recurring sales of test strips, accessories, and potentially bundled subscription services for data analysis or follow-up testing.. Assumptions: Consumers trust DIY testing results enough to act on them; Price sensitivity is manageable for a premium product; Distribution channels (hardware stores, online) are accessible to target consumers. Predictions: Willingness to pay for a premium test kit will exceed the cost of a single test; Repeat purchase rate for test strips will be higher than for one-time use; Consumer surveys will show intent to purchase a home water testing kit within the next 12 months.

T2: Consumers will adopt home water testing kits because they need to comply with local water quality regulations or safety standards, making DIY testing a legal requirement rather than a voluntary choice. Who benefits: Homeowners and renters in regions with strict water quality laws who must test their water to ensure compliance.. Why behaviour changes: Regulatory pressure and the need to avoid fines or legal action create a mandatory need for accurate water testing, shifting behavior from voluntary to required.. How value is captured: Hach can capture value through compliance-focused sales of test kits, accessories, and potentially subscription services for regulatory reporting.. Assumptions: Regulatory bodies enforce water quality testing in target regions; Consumers are aware of and comply with these regulations; Hach's products meet the required standards for regulatory compliance. Predictions: Sales of compliance-focused test kits will increase in regions with strict water quality laws; Consumers will purchase kits at higher volumes when marketed as required by regulation; Regulatory bodies will report increased adoption of DIY testing kits in compliance regions.

A poor water quality result by a kit should be confirmed with follow-up analyses by a laboratory that uses state-of-the-art instruments, certified methods, and quality control measures to ensure accuracy and reliability.". Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Home Water Test Kits" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a sample of homeowners and renters in regions with varying water quality regulations. Participants are offered a mock premium test kit at two price points: $20 (one-time test) and $40 (reusable strips and accessories). They are asked: (1) How likely are they to purchase the kit? (2) What would be the maximum price they would pay for a reusable version? (3) Why would they choose to purchase? (open-ended).. Sample: 500 respondents (200 in regions with strict water quality laws, 200 in regions with moderate laws, 100 in regions with few regulations). Recruit via online panels to match demographic distribution.. Measure: Share of respondents indicating "high" likelihood to purchase at each price point, plus average maximum price willingness to pay for a reusable version.. Predictions: T1: Higher willingness to pay and purchase intent at the $40 price point than at $20, especially in regions with strict regulations.; T2: Purchase intent and willingness to pay are similar across price points and do not differ by regulatory region.. Decision rule: If the share of respondents indicating "high" likelihood to purchase at $40 exceeds 30% and exceeds the share at $20 by at least 5 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on peace-of-mind monitoring. If the difference is less than 5 percentage points, consider a lower-priced entry product or maintain B2B focus. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a consumer proposition.. Cost: 12000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence shows home water test kits are widely available and sold under Hach brands, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or regulatory requirement. Conduct the proposed willingness-to-pay survey to test T1 vs. T2 before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or regulatory requirements for home water test kits. Therefore it provides no support or contradiction to T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence shows home water test kits are widely available and sold under Hach brands, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or regulatory requirement. Conduct the proposed willingness-to-pay survey to test T1 vs. T2 before committing resources. Target customer: Individual homeowners and renters who are concerned about water quality but currently rely on utility or professional testing.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that provides peace-of-mind monitoring of drinking water quality through a premium test kit and accessories, leveraging Hach’s existing brand credibility and distribution.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the 12‑week, €12,000 willingness-to-pay survey with 500 respondents to measure purchase intent and price sensitivity at two price points.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, actual purchase intent, willingness to pay for a premium product, and the extent to which regulatory requirements drive demand remain uncertain.. Would change if: If the survey shows purchase intent at $40 exceeds 30% and is at least 5 percentage points higher than at $20, indicating strong demand for peace-of-mind monitoring.; If new evidence shows that regulatory bodies in target regions actively require DIY water testing, supporting T2.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Test "Messaging Test: Insurance vs Lifestyle Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Run a targeted online survey with two message variants for a home CPR device. Participants are recruited from two distinct geographic segments: a segment with strong insurance or legal requirements for home CPR training (e.g., California, New York) and a segment without such requirements (e.g., Texas). Each participant sees one of the two message variants and is asked to indicate their purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely).. Sample: 500 adults (250 from each segment) to ensure sufficient statistical power.. Measure: Purchase intent score on a 7-point scale for each message variant.. Predictions: T1: In the segment with insurance/legal requirements, the purchase intent score for the insurance message will be significantly higher than for the lifestyle message.; T2: In the segment without insurance/legal requirements, the purchase intent score for the lifestyle message will be significantly higher than for the insurance message.. Decision rule: If the purchase intent score for the insurance message in the segment with requirements is at least 1.5 points higher than the lifestyle message, proceed to develop a consumer proposition focused on insurance/legal requirements. If the lifestyle message score is at least 1.5 points higher in the segment without requirements, proceed to develop a consumer proposition focused on lifestyle. If neither difference is statistically significant, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Purchase Intent Test: Personal Health Responsibility vs Trust Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a home CPR training kit and are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely). Randomly assigned to either a personal health responsibility message (emphasizing family protection and personal responsibility) or a trust message (emphasizing Laerdal's medical reputation and professional-grade safety).. Sample: 500 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to ensure representativeness.. Measure: Average purchase intent score for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Personal health responsibility message will yield a higher average purchase intent score than trust message.; T2: Trust message will yield a higher average purchase intent score than personal health responsibility message.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for the personal health responsibility condition exceeds the trust condition by at least 1.5 points (e.g., 5.5 vs 4.0), proceed to develop a consumer proposition based on personal health responsibility. If the trust condition exceeds the personal condition by at least 1.5 points, develop a consumer proposition based on trust. If the difference is below 1.5 points, conclude insufficient evidence to justify investment and recommend no expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training, but first run the proposed purchase intent test to validate whether personal health responsibility messaging drives higher purchase intent than trust messaging. If the test confirms a 1.5-point advantage for the personal health responsibility condition, proceed to develop a consumer proposition; otherwise, reconsider the investment. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) measures packing errors for a label printer and does not address consumer purchase intent, personal health responsibility, or trust messaging. Therefore it provides no evidence for or against T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training, but first run the proposed purchase intent test to validate whether personal health responsibility messaging drives higher purchase intent than trust messaging. If the test confirms a 1.5-point advantage for the personal health responsibility condition, proceed to develop a consumer proposition; otherwise, reconsider the investment. Target customer: Individual consumers (households) who are concerned about out-of-hospital cardiac arrests and want to be prepared to perform CPR in emergencies.. Value proposition: A portable, user-friendly home CPR training kit that empowers families to learn lifesaving skills in the comfort of their own home, leveraging Laerdal's medical reputation and personal health responsibility messaging.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the purchase intent test (500 U.S. adults, randomized messaging conditions, 7-point scale, 1.5-point threshold) within the 8-week, €18,000 budget.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and the willingness to pay for a home CPR kit are uncertain. Regulatory approval for consumer use of CPR devices is also uncertain.. Would change if: If the test shows the trust condition exceeds the personal health responsibility condition by at least 1.5 points, we would shift focus to a trust-based consumer proposition.; If the test shows no significant difference or the personal health responsibility condition wins, we would recommend no expansion and continue focusing on B2B markets.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Homeowner Purchase Intent Pilot" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a controlled offer. Participants are recruited from homeowners who have completed a kitchen survey. They are randomly assigned to one of two treatment groups: Group A (customisable model) and Group B (professional-grade model). Both groups see a product description of a Winterhalter undercounter dishwasher with a price point 20% above a standard model. Group A also receives a customisation option and a discount for adding a glassware kit. Participants indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale.. Sample: 300 homeowners recruited via an online panel, 150 per group, balanced for age, income, and kitchen ownership status. Measure: Average WTP (in euros) and purchase intent (on 7-point scale) for each group. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group B, because homeowners value customisation and premium pricing.; T2: Group B will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group A, because homeowners seek a professional-grade, hygienic solution.. Decision rule: If Group A's average WTP is at least 20% higher than Group B's and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), we conclude T1 is supported and recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on customisation and premium pricing. If Group B's average WTP is at least 20% higher than Group A and the difference is statistically significant, we conclude T2 is supported and recommend a professional-grade consumer proposition. If neither difference is statistically significant, we conclude neither theory is strongly supported and recommend no new consumer proposition at this time.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Premium vs. Eco-Premium Consumer Scrubber Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants view a product description of a consumer-grade walk-behind scrubber (identical performance spec but marketed differently). One version is marketed as a premium convenience product (e.g., 'Save time with smart cleaning technology') and the other as an eco‑premium product (e.g., 'Water‑saving and chemical‑free cleaning solution'). Both versions are priced at a 20% premium over a comparable professional model. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑7 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).. Sample: 300 adult consumers in the US and Western Europe, screened for interest in home cleaning and willingness to pay a premium for cleaning equipment.. Measure: Purchase intent (1‑7 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: stated importance of convenience vs. sustainability.. Predictions: T1: Premium version will achieve purchase intent at least 15% higher and higher willingness to pay than eco‑premium version.; T2: Eco‑premium version will achieve purchase intent at least 15% higher and higher willingness to pay than premium version.. Decision rule: If premium version purchase intent ≥ 15% points higher than eco‑premium version AND premium willingness to pay ≥ 20% higher than eco‑premium willingness to pay, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition. If eco‑premium version ≥ 15% points higher, develop an eco‑premium proposition. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into consumer market.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not yet commit to a full consumer proposition. Conduct the proposed premium vs. eco‑premium conjoint test to measure actual purchase intent and willingness to pay. If the premium version meets the 15‑point threshold, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition; if the eco‑premium version meets the threshold, develop an eco‑premium proposition. If neither meets the threshold, maintain the current B2B focus. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Measure: Primary outcome: purchase intent measured as the proportion of participants who indicate they would purchase the kit at the stated price. Decision rule: If purchase intent in Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition. Test "Digital Messaging Test: DIY vs Professional Insulation Proposition" between T1; T2. Method: Run a targeted online survey with two distinct messaging paths. Recruit 1,000 UK homeowners who have completed a home improvement project in the past 12 months. Randomly assign participants to one of two groups: Group A receives a DIY-focused message emphasizing cost savings, environmental impact, and ease of installation; Group B receives a professional guidance message emphasizing expert installation, code compliance, and peace of mind. Both groups are presented with a product description of Kingspan's roof insulation and a price point (e.g., £150 for a 4m² roll). Participants are asked to indicate their purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and to state the primary reason for their choice.. Sample: 1,000 UK homeowners who have completed a home improvement project in the past 12 months, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and primary reason for choosing (open-ended).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and will cite cost savings and environmental impact as the primary reason.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and will cite professional guidance and code compliance as the primary reason.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 5.5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A average >= 5.5 - Group B average), we conclude that T1 is more supported and recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on DIY motivation. If Group B's average is at least 5.5 points higher, we conclude T2 is more supported and recommend a professional guidance proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, we conclude neither theory is strongly supported and recommend further market research.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

sources.excerpt: Designed with the modern workplace and non-commercial segment in mind, the A300 Fresh Brew is the perfect solution for non-commercial spaces such as offices, hospitals, and hotels.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Franke Coffee Systems should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its professional coffee machines, and identify what public evidence would justify that investment.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment; Must consider Franke’s existing professional offerings (fully automatic, semi-automatic, traditional) and its current consumer reach; Must assess demand, competitive landscape, and potential value capture mechanisms. Alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home office, small retail, travel) with a new product or service model; Expand the existing professional line into adjacent consumer segments without a new differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer accessories, subscription services, or new distribution channels); Maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing professional market; no expansion; License Franke’s technology or brand to third‑party consumer product manufacturers rather than creating a direct consumer proposition.

Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from utilitarian purchase decisions to status-driven purchases when a product is framed as a premium, professional-grade item rather than a basic household appliance.. T2: Home office consumers will adopt a differentiated Franke coffee machine if they need a reliable, high-quality coffee solution that reduces daily coffee preparation time, because they value efficiency and consistency in their work environment. Who benefits: Franke Coffee Systems (through increased volume sales and repeat purchases of replacement parts and consumables) and early adopters who seek to streamline their coffee routine.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from utilitarian purchase decisions to efficiency-driven purchases when a product offers faster, more consistent coffee preparation, reducing the time spent on daily coffee tasks.. How value is captured: Franke can capture value through higher unit volume sales, recurring revenue from consumables, and potential partnerships with coffee shop chains or service providers to offer maintenance packages.. Assumptions: Consumers prioritize coffee quality and consistency over brand prestige.; Time savings are a significant purchase driver for home office users.; Franke can demonstrate measurable time savings in product demonstrations or trials.. Predictions: Home office users will rank time savings as a top factor in choosing a coffee machine.; Willingness to pay for a machine that reduces coffee preparation time will be higher than for a machine with similar features but no time-saving claim.; Sales of a differentiated Franke machine will be concentrated among users who already own multiple coffee machines and seek to optimize their workflow..
